title: How to decide between Set and List
shortTitle: How do you decide between Set and List?
keyPoints: List allows duplicates and provides index-based access; Set enforces uniqueness and provides fast contains()
ArrayList.contains() is O(n) – it scans every element; HashSet.contains() is O(1) on average
Use List when insertion order matters, positional access is needed, or duplicates are valid business data
Use Set when each element must be unique and the primary operation is membership testing
LinkedHashSet gives you uniqueness plus insertion order; TreeSet gives uniqueness plus sorted order
In banking: transaction logs are Lists (same amount can repeat, order matters); active account registries are Sets (each account number is unique)

s1_definition.oneliner: Use List when you need ordered, indexed data that may contain duplicates; use Set when each element must be unique and you primarily need fast membership testing.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **List** is an ordered, index-addressable collection that allows duplicates; implementations include `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`, and `CopyOnWriteArrayList`
- **Set** stores only unique elements determined by `equals()` and `hashCode()`; implementations include `HashSet`, `LinkedHashSet`, and `TreeSet`
- The decision rule: can an element appear more than once, and do you need access by position? If yes, choose List. If each element must be unique and you mostly call `contains()`, choose Set
- Both extend `Collection`, so you can pass either to any method that accepts `Collection<T>`
s1_definition.analogy: A List is the bank's transaction log. The same deposit amount can appear many times, and the order matters because auditors need to see transactions chronologically. A Set is the register of unique account numbers. Each account appears exactly once, and the main question the system asks is "does this account exist?" You would never use a List to track unique account numbers because you would have to scan the entire list every time to check for duplicates.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Decision tree: List or Set?

  Can the same element appear more than once?
  ├── YES → Do you need index access (get by position)?
  │         ├── YES → ArrayList
  │         └── NO  → Do you need fast add/remove at ends?
  │                   ├── YES → LinkedList
  │                   └── NO  → ArrayList (default)
  │
  └── NO (unique elements only)
            → Do you need sorted order?
            ├── YES → TreeSet (O(log n) ops)
            └── NO  → Do you need insertion order?
                      ├── YES → LinkedHashSet
                      └── NO  → HashSet (O(1) ops, default)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The choice between List and Set comes down to two questions: can the same element appear more than once, and do you need positional access? If duplicates are valid business data and you need to access elements by index, use a List. If each element must be unique and your primary operation is asking "does this element exist," use a Set.

In the National Bank of India system, Rajesh uses an ArrayList for the transaction history of account SAV2001 because the same deposit amount of 50,000 rupees can appear multiple times, each representing a different event, and auditors need to see transactions in chronological order. For the active account registry, he uses a HashSet because each account number must be unique and the system checks "does this account exist" thousands of times per second. HashSet answers that question in O(1) time, while ArrayList would scan every element.

When you need both uniqueness and ordering, LinkedHashSet gives you insertion order and TreeSet gives you sorted order. When you need uniqueness and concurrency, use `ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()`. Always remember that a Set relies on `equals()` and `hashCode()` – if your class does not override both correctly, two objects with identical data will be treated as different.

Remember one sentence: List is for ordered data with duplicates and index access; Set is for unique data with fast membership testing.
